proposed.explanation: Native species are adapted to specific conditions; transplanting outside those conditions fails. Mangrove species are salt-tolerant and adapted to waterlogged, tidal conditions. Rainforest species require well-drained soils and fresh water. Each has specific physiology and ecological requirements evolved for their ecosystem. Planting rainforest species in a mangrove habitat results in failure; the species cannot survive the salinity and waterlogging. Using ecosystem-appropriate species (many species across multiple ecosystem types) maximizes biodiversity—not reduces it. Ecological restoration is fundamentally based on matching species to ecosystem conditions. Mangrove species are salt-tolerant and adapted to waterlogged, tidal conditions. Rainforest species require well-drained soils and fresh water. Each has specific physiology and ecological requirements evolved for their ecosystem. Planting rainforest species in a mangrove habitat results in failure; the species cannot survive the salinity and waterlogging. Successful restoration matches species to ecosystem type, respecting evolved adaptations to environmental conditions.
